Went to see Kunal today in his rented room near the station. He lost his job three months ago. He's been sleeping on a mat because the landlord took the bed back, and eating mostly bread. I tried to talk about his plans: courses, applications, the future. He just stared at me. 'I don't know about next month, Kamal. I don't even know about tomorrow's lunch.' I realised I'd been thinking he was lazy for not applying anywhere. He isn't lazy. His mind is full of rent and food. There's no room left for plans. So I stopped lecturing. I bought groceries, and I asked my cousin about the shelter with a proper bed near the station. Kunal called me tonight and said he'd slept properly for the first time in weeks. He asked me to help him write his CV tomorrow.

Kamal

passage:
Class 8. Charu started Bharatanatyam classes on Saturdays. Her friends laughed. 'That's for aunties.' She almost quit.

Class 9. Charu practised in her room every evening. Her friend Zeenat asked why she bothered when nobody at school cared. Charu said, 'When I dance, I feel like me.' Zeenat didn't get it but stopped teasing.

Class 10. At the school's annual day, Charu performed alone. Some students sniggered at first. By the end, the hall was silent. Zeenat was the first to clap. Afterwards Charu said, 'I wasn't dancing for them. It's just what fits me.'

qa.q: When did Charu start Bharatanatyam classes?
qa.a: In Class 8.

qa.q: How did Charu feel when she danced?
qa.a: Charu felt truly herself and at peace, even when others laughed.

qa.q: What choice helped Charu most, and why?
qa.a: Continuing to practise every evening despite the teasing, because it kept her close to what felt true for her.

qa.q: How does Zeenat's view of Charu change over the years?
qa.a: Zeenat goes from not understanding to respecting Charu, being the first to clap.

grounding: Over three years, a teenager keeps learning classical dance despite jokes, since it feels true to her, and inner interest outweighs fitting in.

passage: Ujjwal, you want to quit the sitar because your friends call it boring? Let your Disha Bua tell you about 1990. I was fifteen in Varanasi. All my friends were learning film songs. I was learning Hindustani vocal from old Pandit-ji, three evenings a week. They called me 'Granny', because I sang 'old songs'. Once, they hid my tanpura before a school programme. I cried in the bathroom. That night I nearly told my father I'd stop. But then I sat with the tanpura and sang Bhairav, and I felt like I'd come home. I thought, if I stop, it's to please them, not me. So I didn't stop. Forty years later, I still sing every morning. Those friends? They still hum film songs. And they come to my concerts.

qa.q: What did Disha's friends call her?
qa.a: 'Granny', for singing 'old songs'.

qa.q: How did Disha feel singing Bhairav that night?
qa.a: Disha felt calm and at home, as if she had come back to herself.

qa.q: What turning point inside the story kept Disha singing?
qa.a: Realising that stopping would only please her friends, not herself, which made her choose her own interest.

qa.q: How might Disha's friends have felt hiding the tanpura?
qa.a: They probably thought it was a harmless joke and didn't realise how much it hurt her.

grounding: An elder recalls keeping up classical singing despite friends' jokes because it felt true to her, choosing inner interest over fitting in.

passage: In the placement cell at the IIT campus, Avni sat across from Rukmini Ma'am, the placement officer. On the desk lay two offers. One from a famous consulting firm, a salary everyone talked about. The other from a small NGO building water systems in villages, paying a third. 'Are you sure, Avni?' Rukmini Ma'am asked. 'Your parents will ask why.' Avni's hands were cold. Her heart was racing. She had dreamed of water work since she saw the dry wells in her grandmother's village. 'I'm scared,' she admitted. 'But when I imagine the consulting job, I feel nothing. When I imagine the villages, I feel calm.' She signed the NGO letter. Rukmini Ma'am smiled. 'Then that's your answer.'

qa.q: What does the NGO do?
qa.a: It builds water systems in villages.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling when she signed the NGO letter?
qa.a: Avni felt scared and also calm, since the NGO work fitted her values.

qa.q: What helped Avni decide, and could others use it?
qa.a: Imagining each job and noticing which one brought calm; others could ask which path feels true to them, not just which pays more.

qa.q: How might Avni's parents react to her choice?
qa.a: Her parents may be surprised or worried about the lower salary, but could also be proud of her reasons.

grounding: A young adult turns down a famous, high-paying job for work that fits her values, and feels both fear and calm.

passage:
Dear Bhupen Chacha,

I wanted to tell you before you hear it from the family. I turned down the offer from the bank in Mumbai. Yes, the big one, with the salary Papa told everyone about. I've taken a job at a small school for children with hearing difficulties in Hubli. The pay is much less. Papa is upset. Honestly, I'm scared. But when I visited the school last month and a little boy signed 'thank you' to me, I felt something I've never felt in an interview. Calm. Like I fit. You once told me that the best work is where you forget to check the clock. I think this is that. Please be on my side at Diwali.

With love,
Manjula

passage: Zainab, you asked on the podcast why I turned down the job at the famous tech company. I'm Binita. It was a dream offer. My friends were jealous. My mother cried with happiness. And I said no. I took a job with a small team making farming apps for tribal cooperatives in Odisha, at less than half the pay. Was I scared? Terrified. I lay awake for a week. But every time I pictured the tech job, I felt a kind of emptiness. When I pictured sitting with the farmers, working out their problems, I felt calm, like the path fitted me. People clap for the famous name. But the clapping isn't what I have to live with every day. The work is.

qa.q: Where does Binita's new team make farming apps for?
qa.a: For tribal cooperatives in Odisha.

qa.q: How did Binita feel after turning down the tech job?
qa.a: Binita felt terrified, lying awake for a week, but also calm about the new path.

qa.a: Picturing daily life in each job and choosing the one that felt calm and fitting, rather than the one that got applause.

qa.q: How might Binita's mother have felt about the decision?
qa.a: Binita's mother, who cried with happiness at the offer, may have felt confused or disappointed at first.

passage: Kunal had been Vinita's teaching assistant in the college chemistry lab for a year, and she noticed things. Most students left the moment the bell rang. Kunal stayed. He was always tinkering with the old spectrometer, asking questions that weren't on the syllabus. One evening she found him still there at eight, trying to measure the colour of turmeric water. 'Is this for your project?' 'No, ma'am. I just want to know why it changes in soap.' Vinita watched his face light up as he explained. His parents wanted him to do an MBA. She didn't argue with that. But she gave him a key to the lab on Saturdays and lent him her old books on dyes. 'Do what makes you curious,' she said. 'Let's see where it goes.'

qa.q: What was Kunal trying to measure at eight in the evening?
qa.a: The colour of turmeric water.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling as she watched Kunal explain?
qa.a: Vinita felt pleased and curious, seeing real passion light up his face.

qa.q: What did Vinita do that others mentoring a young person could copy?
qa.a: She gave him space and tools, a lab key and books, rather than pushing him towards a set career.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel with the Saturday lab key?
qa.a: Kunal would likely feel trusted and excited, free to follow his curiosity.

grounding: A mentor notices a student light up and stay late for his own interest, not marks, and gives him space and tools.

passage:
'Noor, it's past seven. The studio's closing.'
'Five more minutes, Kavitha Ma'am. The glaze isn't right.'
'It's not for marks. The assignment was last week.'
'I know. I just want to see what happens if I add more ash.'
Kavitha put down her keys. 'Show me.'
Noor held up three cups, each a slightly different green. 'This one looks like monsoon moss.'
'It does.' Kavitha smiled. 'Your parents want you to do design management, don't they?'
'Yes. It's safer.'
'I won't tell you what to do. But I've seen your face with clay.' She pulled out a spare key. 'The studio's free on Sunday mornings. And I have glaze books you can borrow.'
Noor's eyes widened. 'Really?'
'Really.'

qa.a: Kavitha probably felt curious and pleased, noticing Noor's genuine engagement with the glaze.

qa.q: What did Kavitha do that supported Noor's interest?
qa.a: She offered Sunday studio time and glaze books without pressing Noor towards any particular career.

qa.q: How does Noor react to Kavitha's offer?
qa.a: Noor is surprised and delighted, eyes widening at the chance.

passage: I've coached debate at the college in Lucknow for fifteen years. I'm Sharmila, and I've seen plenty of students who want trophies. Parveen was different. She stayed after practice, not to prepare for competitions, but to read old speeches and argue about ideas with me. She'd light up when she found a good argument, even one she disagreed with. Her family wanted her in law. I didn't push her away from that. But I gave her my library card, and asked if she'd like to run a reading circle for juniors. She did, and it grew to twenty students. She's now doing a master's in philosophy. I didn't make that choice for her. I only made sure she had room to follow what lit her up.

qa.q: How many students joined Parveen's reading circle?
qa.a: Twenty students.

qa.q: What did Sharmila feel watching Parveen stay after practice?
qa.a: Sharmila felt pleased and curious, seeing Parveen light up over ideas, not trophies.

qa.q: What did Sharmila give Parveen that others could offer a curious young person?
qa.a: Space and tools: a library card and the chance to run a reading circle, without pressing a career.

qa.q: How might Parveen's family have felt about her choosing philosophy?
qa.a: Her family, who wanted law, might have been surprised or worried, but perhaps proud too.
